Richardson's ground squirrels (Urocitellus richardsonii) display a distinctive life history strategy shaped by their short active season in the northern Great Plains. Newborn pups emerge from a gestation period lasting approximately 24 days [tg = approximately 24 days] when maternal body temperature is maintained at 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C], a remarkably brief intrauterine development for a rodent of this body size. The neonatal wet weight at birth averages 6.35 grams [Wwb = 6.35 grams], a modest starting mass that reflects the altricial condition typical of many ground-dwelling sciurids. This limited initial investment is offset by rapid postnatal growth fueled by rich milk provisions during the subsequent nursing phase. Litter sizes are substantial, with females typically producing around six pups per litter [N_R_i = around six pups per litter], a reproductive output that necessitates considerable maternal energy expenditure during the short summer window. Juveniles then enter a period of rapid somatic growth that continues through their first summer, building the body reserves necessary for overwinter survival. Mortality during this post-weaning phase can be high, particularly in years of drought or late-season frost that reduce forage quality. The timing of weaning is thus closely tied to local phenological conditions, with females adjusting reproductive schedules to maximize offspring survival prospects.

This adult mass is reached after the completion of several months of active feeding and fat deposition, a critical preparation for the prolonged hibernation period that can last over half the year. Fat stores accumulated during late summer are the primary energy source sustaining individuals through torpor, and variations in pre-hibernation body mass significantly influence overwinter survival rates. Males typically emerge from hibernation slightly heavier than females, a dimorphism that may confer advantages during the intense scramble competition for mates that follows spring emergence. The asymptotic mass is relatively consistent across populations, though local forage availability can introduce modest geographic variation, with individuals from more productive sites occasionally exceeding typical values.

The attainment of sexual maturity coincides with the completion of substantial somatic growth, ensuring that first-time breeders have sufficient body reserves to support gestation and lactation. Age at first reproduction in wild populations is almost invariably one year, a timing that reflects strong selective pressure to maximize lifetime reproductive output within a limited lifespan.
